parts.title: Volunteering abroad
parts.context: A student asks about a volunteering project in Peru.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a student phoning an organisation about volunteering abroad. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: Global Helpers, Rosa speaking.

script.speaker: jake
script.text: Hello. I'm interested in volunteering abroad this summer. I'd like to find out how it works.

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: Great. I'll take some details first, and then I'll explain the projects.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The caller wants to volunteer abroad, so 'abroad' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: Could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: jake
script.text: Jake Holmes. That's H-O-L-M-E-S.

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: Thank you, Jake. How old are you?

script.speaker: jake
script.text: I'm twenty.

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: And what do you do?

script.speaker: jake
script.text: I'm a student. I'm studying geography at university, and I'd like to do something useful in the holidays.

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: Do you have a country in mind?

script.speaker: jake
script.text: Peru, because I speak some Spanish, and I've always wanted to see the Andes.

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: And when would you be available?

script.speaker: jake
script.text: From June, once my exams have finished.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: We have several projects in Peru. The most popular is building a clinic for a mountain village, where the nearest doctor is a day's walk away.

script.speaker: jake
script.text: That sounds worthwhile. How long does it last?

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: Eight weeks. We also have shorter projects, but the clinic needs a long commitment, because the building takes time.

script.speaker: jake
script.text: What's the cost? I know that volunteers usually pay something.

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: Yes, there's a fee that covers accommodation and food, which we'll explain. To reserve a place, you pay a deposit of ninety-five pounds, which is deducted from the fee.

script.speaker: jake
script.text: Do I need any vaccinations?

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: Yes, you'll need to check with your doctor, but the one that's compulsory is yellow fever, because of the region you'll be visiting.

script.speaker: jake
script.text: And what's the deadline for applying?

script.speaker: rosa
script.text: The thirty-first of March. After that, the places are usually full, and we start a waiting list.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: University accommodation
parts.context: An accommodation officer describes the halls of residence at an open day.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear an accommodation officer giving a talk to prospective students at a university open day. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: hale
script.text: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to the open day. I'm Gareth Hale, the accommodation officer, and I'll tell you about the halls of residence, because first-year students are guaranteed a place.

script.speaker: hale
script.text: Ashdown Hall is the closest to the library, only a two-minute walk, so it's the favourite with students who like to study late. It's also where the older students tend to live.

script.speaker: hale
script.text: Birch Court has the most comfortable rooms, and all of them have private bathrooms, which is a big attraction. It's also the quietest hall, and the most expensive.

script.speaker: hale
script.text: Cedar House is the cheapest option, and it's popular with students on a tight budget. The rooms are small, but the community is friendly, and it has a large kitchen on every floor.

script.speaker: hale
script.text: Dunmore Lodge has its own gym and a swimming pool, which residents can use free. And Elm Park is the newest building, only two years old, with modern rooms and the best wifi on the campus.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: hale
script.text: Now, some practical information. To be sure of a room, you must apply by the first of July, and not the first of August as it says in some of the older leaflets. After that, we allocate rooms in the order that we receive applications.

script.speaker: hale
script.text: The campus is about three miles from the city centre. There's a bus every ten minutes, and it's free for students, so most people never need a car.

script.speaker: hale
script.text: The rent includes bills, such as electricity and heating, and also internet access, so there are no nasty surprises. Meals are not included, except in Birch Court, where breakfast is provided.

script.speaker: hale
script.text: Contracts last for forty-two weeks, which covers the whole academic year, including most of the holidays. If you want to leave earlier, you must give four weeks' notice.

script.speaker: hale
script.text: Finally, if you'd like to share with a friend, you should apply together, using the same reference number, and we'll do our best to put you next to each other. I'll be here all afternoon for questions.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: An experiment on multitasking
parts.context: Two psychology students discuss the results of their experiment.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two psychology students, Cara and Dev, discussing an experiment on multitasking. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: cara
script.text: Dev, I've been through the results of our multitasking experiment. Some of them surprised me.

script.speaker: dev
script.text: Me too. The one I didn't expect was that the people who said they were good at multitasking actually performed worst.

script.speaker: cara
script.text: And I didn't expect the age result. We assumed younger participants would do better, because they're used to using several screens at once, but they did no better than the older ones.

script.speaker: dev
script.text: Did the music make a difference? I expected it would.

script.speaker: cara
script.text: It didn't, no. The task took about as long as we'd planned, and the women and the men performed the same.

script.speaker: dev
script.text: How many participants did we have in the end?

script.speaker: cara
script.text: Forty-eight. We planned for sixty, but twelve dropped out.

script.speaker: dev
script.text: And what was the main task?

script.speaker: cara
script.text: Memorising a list of words, while answering simple questions that appeared on the screen.

script.speaker: dev
script.text: We measured both errors and the time taken, didn't we?

script.speaker: cara
script.text: Yes, both, and the results agreed with each other.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: cara
script.text: What do you think the results show?

script.speaker: dev
script.text: That the brain doesn't really do two things at once. It switches quickly between them, and each switch costs a little time, and causes errors.

script.speaker: cara
script.text: That fits the theory. What limitations should we mention?

script.speaker: dev
script.text: That the experiment was done in a laboratory, which isn't realistic. In real life, people multitask in noisy, distracting places.

script.speaker: cara
script.text: So for future research, we'd recommend including real-life tasks, such as writing emails while answering the phone.

script.speaker: dev
script.text: I agree. Shall I analyse the error data tonight?

script.speaker: cara
script.text: Please. I'll draft the introduction.

script.speaker: dev
script.text: And when is the report due?

script.speaker: cara
script.text: On Monday, so we have the weekend.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: the physics of musical instruments
parts.context: A physics lecture on how instruments make sound.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about the physics of musical instruments. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning. Whether it's a violin, a flute or a drum, every musical instrument works on the same principle: it produces sound by making something vibrate. Today I'll explain the physics behind that.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The first idea is pitch, which means how high or low a note sounds. Pitch depends on frequency, that is, how many vibrations occur each second. The faster the vibration, the higher the note.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Take a stringed instrument. A shorter string vibrates faster, so it produces a higher note. That's why a guitarist presses a string against the fingerboard, to shorten the part that vibrates. Tightening a string also raises the note, and a thicker string vibrates more slowly, so it gives a lower note, which is why the bass strings of a guitar are thicker.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: In a wind instrument, such as a flute, what vibrates is a column of air inside the tube. A longer column vibrates more slowly, so the note is lower. Opening holes along the tube makes the column effectively shorter, which raises the pitch.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: A string on its own makes very little sound, because it moves very little air. That's why instruments have a body. The wooden body of a guitar or a violin vibrates along with the strings, and amplifies the sound through a process called resonance.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Why does a trumpet sound different from a violin, even when they play the same note? Because each instrument produces not just the main note but also a mixture of higher notes, called harmonics, and the mixture is different for each instrument. This is what gives each its own character.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Another useful fact is that if you double the frequency of a note, you raise it by one octave. Orchestras normally tune to the note A, which has a frequency of four hundred and forty hertz.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: And percussion? A drum produces sound when its stretched skin is struck, and vibrates. A tighter skin gives a higher note. Next week we'll look at the physics of the human voice.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
